The other side of the conflict, and the more important half. A globally-active 'Shreyaa Bhattacharya' shares a first name with an Outlook-scoped 'Shreya Menon'. In Outlook the client's name is already correct and must survive untouched - a system that pulled it toward the higher-confidence colleague would rename the user's client in an email to that client. Replaces an earlier version of this case that asked the system to correct the formatter's output using ASR text it had already discarded; that was a formatter bug dressed up as a memory case.

A romanisation the recogniser has never produced for this person and that is in no variant table. 'Aadhith' and 'Aadith' share no metaphone key until the fold collapses aspiration (dh~d), at which point both become 'adit' and land in one blocking bucket. The other half of the same class, and the reason the system has three verdicts rather than two. 'Eeshan' is phonetically close enough to retrieve but not close enough to act on (similarity 0.87 against an apply bar of 0.91). Surfacing it as a suggestion is the honest answer: one confirmation turns it into an observed variant and it applies silently thereafter, which is exactly the 'fix it once' loop. A two-valued system has to either guess or stay silent here.

Devanagari in, Devanagari out. The variant differs from the canonical only in vowel length (मि vs मी), which the script marks and casual dictation does not respect. Nothing about the pipeline is English-specific: the text is transliterated to a Latin phonetic form, folded, and keyed exactly as a romanised name would be.

PASS B15-001 no_candidate expect abstain correct_abstention

The majority of real traffic: nothing here should be touched. Note the reason is below_threshold rather than no_candidate, and that is an honest cost being recorded. Once memory holds a three-letter acronym like WER, the word 'we' shares a blocking key with it and the gate opens on a great many ordinary sentences. Retrieval then finds nothing worth acting on. The guarantee that survives is the one that matters - nothing changes and no model is called - and the cost is one index probe. [Updated when the romanisation fold was widened to collapse p/ph/f and y/i: this sentence's tokens no longer share a blocking key with anything in memory, so the gate now closes before retrieval instead of opening and declining. The output is unchanged and the call is now free rather than merely correct - a strictly better result, recorded as it behaves.]

The decisive negative for multilingual support, and the reason cross-script RETRIEVAL and cross-script REWRITING are different things. The memory holds this colleague as 'Aadith Narayanan' and the phonetic index genuinely matches the Devanagari spelling - that is deliberate, so one person does not become two half-learned entries. But splicing a Latin name into the middle of a Hindi sentence is not a spelling correction, it is an alphabet change, and nothing in the evidence says the user wanted one.

Small edit distance to a known lexeme, entirely different referent.
